```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```


``` {r message = F, warning = F}
# Load packages
library(tidyverse) # note: tidyverse includes ggplot2

# STEP 1: Loading the data

# Import the original CSV files
covar <- read_csv("../Data/GSE85307_covar.csv")
gene_expr <- read_csv("../Data/GSE85307_geneExpression.csv")
gene_names <- read_csv("../Data/GSE85307_geneNames.csv")
```

### Initial Data Inspection
```{r}

# STEP 2: Inspecting the data

# Checking how many rows and columns are there in each file
dim(covar)      # RESULT: 157 X 10
dim(gene_expr)  # RESULT: 500 X 158
dim(gene_names) # RESULT: 750 X 2

# Checking what the column names are
#names(covar)
#names(gene_expr)  # column names seem to match the geoID in covar
#names(gene_names) # contains a Probe ID and Name....will likely use this probe ID
# to match gene expression with gene name...gene expression columns seem to be 
# like probe ID

# Viewing a few rows of each dataset
#head(covar)
#head(gene_expr[,1:6]) # looking at first 6 columns
#head(gene_names)

# Viewing each dataset fully
#View(covar)
#View(gene_expr)
#View(gene_names)

```

Since NFYC was selected as the first gene in Submission 1, we now need to select 
two additional genes for Submission 2. The gene name dataset contains the 
gene names and their corresponding probe IDs, while the gene expression dataset 
contains the expression values associated with those probe IDs. We will look 
select these two additional genes by looking at genes which are present in both
the gene name data set and the gene expression dataset.So this mean that the probe
ids for the genes should be present in both the datasets (in the PROBEID column
of gene names dataset and in the ...1 column of the gene expressiond dataset)

```{r}
# STEP 3: Identifying genes available in both datasets and picking two more (in 
# addition to NFYC)

# Finding gene names whose probe IDs are also present in the gene expression 
# dataset
availableGenes <- gene_names[gene_names$PROBEID %in% gene_expr$...1, ]

# Looking at some of these genes 
head(availableGenes, 10)

```
So, the two additional genes I will pick are SOCS5 (sounds like sock) and HAUS4 
(sounds like house). I chose these genes because they represent different biological 
functions when taken together with NFYC. NFYC is involved in transcriptional 
regulation (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gene/4802). SOCS5 is involved in regulating 
the cellular signalling pathway (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/O75159/entry). 
HAUS4 is involved in microtubule organization and cell division 
(https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gtr/genes/54930/). Examining these three genes
for the same maternal characteristics can be interesting as we can see whether these
characteristics differ at all across genes with different biological functions.

Now that I have picked the two additional genes, SOCS5 and HAUS4, I will need to 
extract the expression values for all three genes (NFYC, SOCS5, and HAUS4) from 
the gene expression dataset. I will then combine these expression values with the 
covariate dataset so that I can look at how the expression of each gene relates 
to the same maternal characteristics.

I will begin this process by first making the specific gene name + probeID dataset
followed by then joining this with the gene expression info for the genes and then
joining it with the covariate data for these genes. 
```{r}
# STEP 5: Creating specific gene name + probe ID dataset

# Creating a list of the 3 selected genes
selectedGenes <- c("NFYC", "SOCS5", "HAUS4")

# Identifying and storing probe IDs + names corresponding to the three selected 
# genes
selectedGenesInfo <- availableGenes[availableGenes$GENE %in% selectedGenes, ]

# Viewing the selected genes and their corresponding probe IDs
# selectedGenesInfo

```

Since the gene expression dataset has probe IDs in its first column and sample 
IDs as the remaining column names, I will use the probe IDs to extract the 
expression values for each gene (so selecting specific rows). 

```{r}
# STEP 6: Creating a dataset consisting of expression values for the selected 
# genes

# Selecting the expression data
selectedGeneExpr <- gene_expr[gene_expr$...1 %in% selectedGenesInfo$PROBEID, ]

# Adding in the gene names
selectedGeneExpr <- selectedGeneExpr %>% 
  left_join(selectedGenesInfo, by = c("...1" = "PROBEID"))

# selectedGeneExpr # Looks good! but gene name is in the last column...we will
# change that using relocate [https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/relocate.html]

selectedGeneExpr <- selectedGeneExpr %>%
  relocate(GENE, .after = ...1) # much better!

# selectedGeneExpr
```

Now, we will reshape the data and convert from wide -> long format
```{r}
# STEP 7: Reshaping gene expression data from wide to long format

# Convert the expression data from wide format to long format, and also removing
# the prove ID column since we don't need that anymore
selectedGeneExprLong <- selectedGeneExpr %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(...1, GENE),
               names_to = "geoID",
               values_to = "Expression") %>%
  select(GENE, geoID, Expression)

# Viewing the reshaped data
# head(selectedGeneExprLong) # Looks good!

```

Now, we will join with the covariate info
```{r}

# STEP 8: Joining gene expression data with covariate data
selectedGeneExprLong <- selectedGeneExprLong %>%
  left_join(covar, by = "geoID")

# Viewing the combined dataset
head(selectedGeneExprLong) # Looks good!
```

Now, we will reshape the data so that each gene has its own expression column.

```{r}
# STEP 9: Long -> Wide so that each gene has its own expression column

selectedGeneExprWide <- selectedGeneExprLong %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = GENE,
              values_from = Expression) 

# Viewing the now wide dataset
head(selectedGeneExprWide) # looks good! gene expression data is added to the end
# so last three columns have the gene expression data. [also we have 13 columns 
# which is as expected since covar had 10 columns and then we added 3 columns for 
# our 3 genes so 13 makes sense]

```

Now, we will again clean our data like we did in Submission 1.
```{r}
# STEP 11: Cleaning the data by checking for any missing values, duplicates, etc.

# Checking the no. of missing values in each column
colSums(is.na(selectedGeneExprWide)) # RESULT: 0 for all columns which means that 
# there are no NAs present in our dataset.

# Checking for duplicated rows
sum(duplicated(selectedGeneExprWide)) # RESULT: 0 which means that there are no 
# duplicated rows

# Checking for duplicate sample IDs
sum(duplicated(selectedGeneExprWide$geoID)) # RESULT: 0 which means that there are 
# no duplicated sample IDS

```

Now that we have checked that there are no NAs and duplicated rows, we will now
focus on cleaning up the column values.
```{r}
# STEP 12: Cleaning up the columns

# Taking a look at the data again so that we know what to put down for our mutate()
#head(selectedGeneExprWide)

# Creating a copy so our new genes dataset remains unchanged
cleanGenesData <- selectedGeneExprWide

# Removing descriptive labels (using gsub) and converting to numerical variables 
# where appropriate (using as.numeric())
cleanGenesData <- cleanGenesData %>%
  mutate(
    # Removing both descriptive labels and converting to numeric (so it is treated 
    # as such)
    mat_age_yrs = as.numeric(gsub("age_years: ",
                                  "", mat_age_yrs)),
    delivery_gestAge_wks = as.numeric(gsub("gestation_weeks: ", 
                                           "", delivery_gestAge_wks)),
    sampleCollection_gestAge_wks = as.numeric(gsub("blood_draw_at_gestation_week: ", 
                                                   "", sampleCollection_gestAge_wks)),
    mat_BMI = as.numeric(gsub("bmi_kg/m2: ", 
                              "", mat_BMI)),  
    # because parentheses are not treated as literal characters and are treated 
    # specially in regular expressions, we add \\ to them so that R treats them 
    # as being literal parentheses.
    mat_vitD = as.numeric(gsub("vitamind_25\\(0h\\)_ng/ml_whole_blood_baseline: ", 
                               "", mat_vitD)),          

    # Only removing descriptive labels
    preg_preeclampsia = gsub("pregnancy_condition: ","", preg_preeclampsia),
    batch_Microarray = gsub("microarray_hybridization_date: ", "", batch_Microarray),
    
    # Removing descriptive labeling and converting 0 to Healthy and 1 to Asthmatic
    mat_asthma = gsub("asthma_0=healthy_1=asthmatic: ", "", mat_asthma),
    mat_asthma = ifelse(mat_asthma=="0", "Healthy", "Asthmatic"))

# Taking a look at our data to see if it looks good. 
head(cleanGenesData) # RESULT: Looks good! Much neater and cleaner.
```
Now that we have cleaned up within the columns, we will do another check to see 
if there is any missing data, i.e., if anything became NA. If we did it 
correctly, we will see no NA values because our dataset didn't have any NA values 
to begin with.

```{r}
# STEP 13: Verifying that we don't have any missing values after cleaning 

# Checking the no. of missing values in each column
colSums(is.na(cleanGenesData)) # RESULT: 0 for all columns which means that there are 
# no NAs present in our dataset.

```

Great, there is no missing data in our cleaned dataset so our dataset is now ready 
to be used for plotting.
